Trump’s Commerce Department is turning $2 billion in CHIPS subsidies into equity stakes in nine quantum-computing firms. And when the government hands out subsidies, takes ownership stakes, and signals which firms are inside the favored circle, markets become distorted by political considerations.
ow.ly/ozuF50Z4rJs

“Power tends to corrupt.” 

In reality, there are only two political philosophies: liberty and power. It is the exercise of power, not freedom, that requires justification, and those who advocate coercion in any arena must bear a heavy burden of proof.

The new DHS green card policy is a radical expansion of its “quiet quitting” on legal immigration, which has been going on for months, says Cato’s @David_J_Bier. 

Before this new policy, DHS had already slashed green card approvals by about 50%.

ow.ly/KQp350Z4rws

Republicans' 2025 tax bill mixes two opposing philosophies: lower rates on a broad base and targeted carve-outs for favored groups. Every new exception shifts the burden elsewhere. A simpler, neutral code remains the better path, explains Cato’s @adamnmichel.
ow.ly/w9B550Z4mK5

Congress prevents physician-owned hospitals from capturing excessive Medicare subsidies on the same basis as other hospitals. Ending the ban would expand government, not limit it.
ow.ly/BjQN50Z4kgO

$59 billion in compliance costs. 28 million privacy violations. 275 leads. That's the Bank Secrecy Act in a single year. 

Cato's @EconWithNick testified before Congress: we have a problem — and it's time to fix it.

ow.ly/AX2N50Z3nQ0

California’s $20 fast-food minimum wage hike killed roughly 18,000 jobs and pushed up restaurant prices. 

In a new Cato Podcast episode, @MrRBourne talks to UC San Diego economist @jeffreypclemens about California’s wage-floor experiment—and the broader lessons for state and federal minimum wage policy.
 
Listen on Spotify, Apple, and our website.

Spotify: ow.ly/xoJC50Z3mUu 
Apple: ow.ly/pjbk50Z3mUo 
Website: ow.ly/twCp50Z3mUq

The Jones Act makes shipping within the United States more expensive — think of it as a tax on domestic commerce, explains Cato's @cpgrabow.

Learn more about one of America's most costly protectionist laws on our YouTube channel: ow.ly/pAs350Z3gpv

Memorial Day is a time to honor those who gave their lives in service to our country — and to reflect on the cost of war. 

As we pay tribute to the fallen, we also recommit ourselves to the cause of peace. 

Revisit David Boaz's Memorial Day reflections from 2019: ow.ly/OZpi50Z2fah

Looking for something to read as America celebrates 250? “Proclaiming Liberty” by @TimothySandefur revisits the revolutionary year of 1776 through the minds of Adams and Jefferson — and shows why the promise of 1776 is as urgent as ever. 

Order your copy today!

A federal gas tax “holiday” sounds like relief—but it’s pricey and underwhelming. Cato’s Krit Chanwong finds a 90‑day pause could add $11–$14.6 billion to federal deficits while saving drivers an average of less than $3 per fill‑up.
ow.ly/4Qfm50Z3oLa

The case for dollarization in the Americas is not about imposing the dollar but about respecting the choice that Latin Americans have made and make on a daily basis when they use the dollar over their local currencies, experts concluded at a Cato Institute event.

ow.ly/xxSb50Z2WSm

Powering AI and data centers requires more than tweaks. Today's electricity marketplace blocks the capital needed to expand supply quickly. As @SecretaryWright said, "we can massively grow our rate of electricity production, but the system we have today is not conducive to it."

Watch the full discussion on how America can unleash the next energy revolution: 
ow.ly/HiIv50Z1f6i

Video

Presidential pardons are meant as a “safety valve”—but they’re also one of the Constitution’s few completely unchecked powers. Cato’s Dan Greenberg argues that its recent, unprecedented use shows why it may be time to add guardrails onto the pardon power, as many states already have.   
ow.ly/C5gN50Z2Kjv

The US-China summit produced few deliverables and no breakthroughs on Taiwan, Iran, or trade. 

In a new Cato Podcast episode, @clark_packard and Evan Sankey break down what was agreed upon, why rare earths and semiconductors have created a strategic stalemate, and what the US should do before Xi comes to Washington.

Listen on Spotify, Apple, and our website.

Spotify: ow.ly/E8rc50Z3mMV 
Apple: ow.ly/NsiI50Z3mMU 
Website: ow.ly/EPIs50Z3mMW

“Giving money and power to government is like giving whiskey and car keys to teenage boys.” – P. J. O’Rourke. 

P. J. O'Rourke was a libertarian, a satirist, and once dubbed "the funniest writer in America," by the Wall Street Journal. A staunch defender of individual liberty—and good scotch—P. J. wrote 21 books, three of which made the NYT's bestseller list.

Why did the United States launch a war with Iran? Is there an exit strategy, or could this turn into another forever war? What would a realist and restrained foreign policy in the Middle East look like? 

Cato Institute media fellow @RIKKISCHLOTT sits down with @Hoffman8Jon, a research fellow in defense and foreign policy studies at Cato, to discuss the shifting justifications for the Iran war, the economic and military costs incurred over the first three months, and the lessons that Washington

The House improved the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act by scrapping a damaging 7-year forced sale for build-to-rent homes and scaling back other overreach. But the “ban” on large institutional investors remains—likely raising, not lowering, costs, explain Cato scholars.  
ow.ly/WpsB50Z2WK6

A rare window for monetary reform has opened. The incoming Fed Chair wants change — and Cato scholars have five concrete proposals to help Kevin Warsh achieve it.
